feedback: When the child chooses the leaf or gentle coaxing: 'The snail crawled aboard calmly — your gentle choice kept it safe.'
When the child chooses a rough grab: 'See how it pulled into its shell? That startled it. Let's try again — what could you slide in front of it instead?'
At the return step: 'You put it back safely, right next to where you found it, so it won't be stepped on. Now it can get home and keep doing its job.'
activities.intendedInsight: Gentleness is not a rule imposed from outside — watching how the creature reacts to the child's own choice shows that careful handling visibly keeps the minibeast safe and calm.
learnerActions: Present a short scenario: 'You found a snail on the path — what do you do?' Offer choices such as: grab it, let it crawl onto your hand, slide a leaf in front of it, or squash it.

For each choice, show or describe the creature's reaction — a rough grab makes a snail pull into its shell ('that startled it'); sliding a leaf in front lets it calmly crawl aboard so you can lift it safely.
Let the child try again after an unkind choice (a 'rewind') so they can discover the gentle option for themselves.

After handling, have the child observe the minibeast briefly (e.g. in a bug-viewer or on a leaf) and then return it to where it was found. Because this snail was found on a path, where it could be stepped on, put it down in the nearest damp, sheltered plant cover right beside the path, saying 'this is near its home'.
activities.title: The snail on the path: choose and see what happens

feedback: Affirm empathetic replies: 'You listened — you'd slide a leaf under it instead of grabbing. The worm would be safe.'
Keep the character's answers factual: handling, habitat, and the creature's real job, not invented abilities.
activities.intendedInsight: Hearing a creature explain, in its own 'voice', how it wants to be treated and why it matters is intended to build empathy and make the care rules feel personal.
learnerActions: Hold a short spoken/role-play conversation with a friendly minibeast in role, e.g. a worm that says 'please put me back under my log, that's my home' and explains how to move it gently, or a bee that explains it should only be watched, not touched, because it may sting if it is grabbed.
Let the child ask the creature open questions such as 'why should I care about you?' and have the character answer with real, grounded facts about its job and how to handle it gently.
Encourage the child to respond and decide what they will do differently next time they meet that minibeast.
activities.title: A minibeast tells you how to care for it

feedback: 'Letting it walk onto a leaf is kind — it doesn't frighten the creature.'
'Keeping it in a jar as a pet isn't kind, even though it feels nice — it needs its own home, so we put it back.'
activities.intendedInsight: The child can recognise and justify the kind action across common situations.
learnerActions: Show pairs or sets of actions (grabbing a snail vs. letting it crawl onto a leaf; keeping a creature in a jar vs. returning it home; squashing vs. observing gently) and have the child sort them into kind and unkind.
Ask 'which is the kind thing to do?' and, for each kind choice, ask the child to say why in one sentence.
activities.title: Kind or unkind? Sort the actions (quick check)

feedback: 'You cupped it gently and put it back where you found it — that's exactly how to keep it safe.'
'A butterfly is different again — its wings are easily damaged, so we look without holding. Each creature needs its own gentle care.'
If the child holds too tightly or forgets to return it: 'Loosen your hands so it isn't squeezed — and remember, it needs to go back to its home.'
activities.intendedInsight: Confidence means handling a minibeast calmly and safely, in the way that suits that particular creature, and putting it back — not picking it up roughly with bare hands.
learnerActions: Model and rehearse a gentle 'toolkit' technique with real or pretend tools instead of fingers: a soft paintbrush, a leaf, a pot and a tray, plus a pooter only for tiny insects and only with an adult (not for worms, snails or delicate creatures). Never squash anything.
Practise the physical routine: gently coax the creature onto a paintbrush or leaf, or cup it in a pot, look at it briefly, then return it to the spot it came from.

Talk through how different minibeasts need different care — a butterfly's wings are delicate so you don't hold it, a worm must not be squeezed, a snail should not be tugged from its shell — so 'gentle' means matching the handling to the creature.
Name and talk through fear or disgust calmly ('spiders and worms can feel scary at first — let's look closely and see what it does') so being brave means being calm, not grabbing.
activities.title: Rehearse the gentle handling routine for real
